blocks.content: As our first example of the utility of the Taylor expansion, consider the case where x is a random variable and we wish to determine the expected value of the function f averaged over all x. Generally speaking, the mean value of a function is only equal to the function evaluated at the mean of x in the special cases in which the function is linear in x or x is a constant. Hence, we cannot just directly substitute the sample mean when trying to evaluate the mean of some function of the data. However, we can get around this problem by expanding f about the mean of x, using Equation A1.1 with $ c = \mu_x $, and then taking the expectation,

The last step follows since the derivative terms, evaluated at $ \mu_x $, are really just constants. Further simplification is possible since, by the definition of a mean, $ E(x - \mu_x) = 0 $, and $ E[(x - \mu_x)^2] $ is the expected variance of $ x $, $ \sigma^2(x) $.
